request.system:
You review a blog article an online shop is about to publish. You did not write it. You see the shop, the topic and the search it targets, the shop's products with the checked facts we hold about each (F1, F2…), and the article. Sentences about products end with the facts they rest on in brackets; [G] marks a sentence the writer says is general knowledge.

Score each from 1 to 5:
- grounding: everything said about the shop's products is exactly what the cited facts say, with nothing added, stretched or implied. One product claim the facts do not support caps this at 2. No invented experience ("we tested", customer stories), statistics or studies.
- information_gain: a shopper who searched this would learn something useful and specific, beyond generic filler they could find anywhere. Padding, repetition and vague praise lower it.
- structure: it answers the search early, its sections follow in a sensible order, headings say what is below them, lists and tables are used where they help.
- fit: it suits this shop, its audience and tone, stays on the topic, and does not read as an advert.
5 is excellent, 4 good enough to publish as it is, 3 acceptable with flaws, 2 or 1 not publishable.

List problems: each with the exact sentence quoted and what is wrong, most serious first. Leave the list empty if there are none.

For each general-knowledge sentence you are given (G1, G2…), answer with its reference and whether every number in it is well established and uncontroversial general knowledge that needs no source (accepted true), or not (false), with a short reason.

<article>
Title: How to fit a dog harness so it is comfortable and secure

A well-fitted dog harness is snug enough that your dog cannot back out of it, but loose enough that you can slide two fingers flat under every strap. The chest piece should rest on the breastbone rather than across the shoulders, and nothing should rub behind the front legs. Measure first, fit it with your dog standing, and check it again after the first few walks.

## Measure before you choose a size

Harness sizes are set by chest girth: the widest part of the ribcage, just behind the front legs. Use a soft tape, keep your dog standing square, and take the measurement snug but not tight. Note the neck measurement too, around the base of the neck where a collar would sit.

The [Trailmate Y-Front Harness](P1) comes in sizes XS to XL, chosen by chest girth [F3]. If your dog is still growing, measure again every few weeks rather than buying a size up and hoping.

## Putting it on

Most dogs accept a harness more easily when it goes on calmly, with a treat, than when they are chased round the kitchen. With an over-the-head style, hold the neck loop open, let your dog put their head through, then pass the belly strap behind the front legs and clip it. Loosen everything first, then take up the slack one strap at a time.

The Trailmate Y-Front Harness has four adjustment points [F2]. Work round them in turn rather than pulling a single strap very tight.

## Checking the fit

- Two fingers should slide flat under each strap, and no more.
- The chest piece should sit centred on the breastbone.
- There should be a clear gap behind the front legs, so the belly strap does not rub.
- The shoulders should move freely when your dog walks.

The Trailmate Y-Front Harness has a Y-shaped chest piece that sits clear of the shoulder joints [F1]. Watch your dog walk and trot after fitting: shortened strides or a twisting gait usually mean something is pressing. Check again after a week, as straps settle and coats change with the seasons.

## Front clip or back clip?

A back clip, between the shoulder blades, suits dogs that already walk well on a loose lead. A front clip on the chest turns a pulling dog gently sideways towards you, which makes pulling less rewarding. The Trailmate Y-Front Harness has a front clip on the chest and a back clip between the shoulder blades [F4], so you can move from one to the other as training goes on. It has reflective stitching [F5] and is machine washable at 30°C [F6].

{{P1}}

## Pairing it with a lead

A lead that is too short pulls the harness up when your dog turns, and one that is too long gives you little control near roads. The [Everyday Padded Lead](P2) is 1.8 metres long [F7] and has a neoprene-padded handle [F8]. It also has a traffic handle near the clip [F9], for keeping your dog close at kerbs and gates. See all our [harnesses](L1) and [leads](L2).

{{P2}}

</article>
